key_insight: Noisy quantum hardware leaves backend-specific fingerprints in measurement outcomes, so routing anonymity must be treated as a formal privacy/security property rather than an implicit assumption.
engineering_relevance: For quantum cloud services, backend selection and output post-processing can leak which device or platform was used, creating a practical privacy risk that must be balanced against output utility.
method: Defined a backend-identifiability game to formalize routing anonymity.
Modeled backend identification as a hypothesis-testing problem and derived exponential anonymity decay at the Chernoff rate under passive i.i.d. access.
Used Pauli-transfer-matrix analysis to show identifying fingerprints are typically an intermediate-depth effect.
evidence_signal: Experiments on Amazon Braket across ion-trap and superconducting devices achieved 87–90% classification within superconducting backends and 96–100% across physical platforms, with identifiability persisting after natural post-processing.
watch_item: The utility-anonymity trade-off means removing backend fingerprints can reduce output usefulness, so anonymization must be tuned carefully for each application.
paper_title: Routing Anonymity and Identifiability of Noisy Quantum Hardware
